The manta rays swam fast during this chasing phase of their mating behavior. The males nipped the tip of the left pectoral fin of the female during each copulation event, both of which occurred within one meter of the surface. The mating behavior of the manta rays is divided into the following five steps. Male chases behind the tail of the female, and attacks her several times while chasing her (chasing behavior, step 1). Male nips the tip of the pectoral fin of the female and then the male moves to the ventral surface of the female (nipping behavior, step 2). Male inserts a clasper into the cloaca of the female (copulating behavior, step 3). Male removes the clasper from the cloaca of the female, but maintains his oral hold of her pectoral fin (post-copulating behavior, step 4). Male releases the pectoral fin of the female, setting her free (separating behavior, step 5). The copulation of Manta birostris is of the abdomen-to-abdomen type.
21746: Knowledge of the feeding behavior of sharks is based on a rich history of descriptive studies, and understanding of the feeding mechanism is rooted in anatomy. These works posed as many questions as they answered. Questions about the feeding mechanism and the function of jaw protrusion remain, the degree of stereotypy of prey capture behavior, the role of jaw suspension in feeding, and how a relatively simple morphological system evolved to the current diversity of feeding forms. Research is now addressing these questions. Utilizing anatomical techniques, computer imaging, electromyography and kinematic analysis, models of the feeding apparatus are being proposed. Prey capture behavior appears not to be a modal action pattern, many sharks exhibiting variability and modulatory abilities. Jaw suspension is not clearly related to feeding behavior as was once thought, and our work has revealed evolutionary shifts that influenced the diversity of feeding forms. We are now posed with additional questions of the evolution of suction feeding and the scaling of prey capture kinematics. The feeding behavior and mechanics of elasmobranchs continue to be an exciting and relatively unexplored area that promises to further our understanding of these apex predators and augment our knowledge of lower vertebrate feeding mechanisms.
Department of Biology, University of South Florida, 4202 East Fowler Ave., Tampa, Florida, 33620 U.S.A.
21747: Anuran call properties were classified as static or dynamic based on within-male variability during bouts of calling. Females exert stabilizing or weakly directional selection on static properties, and highly directional selection on dynamic properties. Selection pressure was examined in two call characteristics; a static character (dominant frequency of the whine), and one dynamic character (intervals between whines). Six phonotaxis experiments were conducted with gravid females using synthetic calls. Stimuli presented for both characters are based on the mean and standard deviation of those characters in the study population, to compare preferences between static and dynamic characters. For each character, 3 distinct intervals of variation have been used (1SD, 2SD, and 3SD), that which is translated in 3 different experiments: mean-1.5SD vs. mean-0.5SD, mean-1.5SD vs. mean+0.5SD and mean-1.5SD vs. mean+1.5SD. As expected, preference was strong in the dynamic character, increasing in proportion to the increase in the interval between stimuli. Preference for the static character remained constant. The degree of 'motivation' in the choice made by females was measured as the time taken to make the choice, the number of speakers visited, and the number of females necessary to get 20 valid responses. For both characters an increase in female 'motivation' was observed in proportion to the increase in the interval of variation between stimuli. Furthermore, all these measures of 'motivation' were greater in the dynamic character than the static character.

21748: The response of male Physalaemus pustulosus to conspecific whines of different frequencies was examined. In the first block of playback experiments (fixed response), three types of synthetic stimuli (HFR, MFR, LFR) were used that corresponded to calls of high frequency (mean+2 SD), mid-frequency (mean), and low frequency (mean-2 SD) for the study population. In the second block of interactive playback experiments (relative response) whines of relative frequency to that of the male subject were used: male frequency + 2 SD (HRR), male frequency (MRR), and male frequency - 2 SD (LRR). In the fixed frequency experiments, no modification of male vocal response was observed. However, in the relative frequency experiments, males responded with greater rates of whine production, and above all, with more complex calls (adding secondary notes) to stimuli of similar or higher frequency than to stimuli of lower frequency than their own. In other words, male vocal competition is greater only when competitors have similar or relatively higher whine frequencies to their own, and does not increase when competitors have call frequencies which are at the mean or higher for the population as a whole. Nevertheless, this differential response cannot be explained only as an effect of competition between males of different sizes, given that the relationship between frequency of the whine and male size is very weak.

21749: The Blackbanded sunfish (Enneacanthus chaetodon) could be considered a cosmopolitan species of the Atlantic coastline (except in Virginia and Maryland, where they are an endangered species). E. chaetodon prefers calm lentic waters which are highly vegetated and extremely acidic in nature. This species quickly adapts to captivity and readily shows aggressive behaviors at low densities. The experiment was designed to determine if the onset of agonistic behaviors in E. chaetodon was significantly influenced by size, density, and/or time. Research has indicated that the encroachment of inter individual space and the acclimation period (a function of time) were both shown to be a significant factor for the onset of aggression. Size, however, was not considered a significant factor for the onset of aggression. The onset of submissive behaviors were considered significant related to the relative body size and with the encroachment of inter individual space; yet it was not considered significant in relation to time. The results indicate that the changes in the agonistic behaviors of E. chaetodon occur as a function of time, encounter, and density.
21750: Variation in temperature and hydration may significantly affect the jumping performance of amphibians and therefore their foraging efficiency, habitat selection, survivorship and fitness. We compared locomotor abilities of two neotropical frogs Eleutherodactylus antillensis and E. cochranae. Jumping performance (maximum jumping distance) was measured at three temperatures (20°C, 25°C and 30°C) and two hydration levels (100% and 75%). E. antillensis showed a significant decrease in jumping ability under dehydration condition at 25°C and 30°C. However at 20°C, there was no significant decrease in jumping ability for E. antillensis. E. cochranae showed no differences in jumping ability. E. cochranae seems to have greater tolerance to changes in temperature and hydration.
Department of Biology, University of Puerto Rico, San Juan, PR 00931-3360
21751: The ability to detect chemical cues is an important predator avoidance mechanism in many organisms, which is best known in aquatic organisms. Only a few studies have examined this ability in terrestrial salamanders. In this experiment, I investigated the response (i.e., avoidance or non-avoidance) of ravine salamanders (Plethodon richmondi) to substrates marked with chemical cues from the tails of autonomized conspecifics. Trials were conducted in 13cm x 2cm glass petri dishes, each dish contained a substrate that was marked with either homogenized tail, autonomized tail, non-injured conspecific or aged water. Salamanders tended to avoid substrates marked with homogenized and autonomized tails and did not avoid substrates marked by non-injured salamanders and aged water. These results suggest that chemical alarm cues can be released from the tails of ravine salamanders and these cues can be detected and avoided.

21752: The advertisement call of Pelodytes punctatus is composed of two distinct pulsed notes (A & B). A single A note is always emitted at the beginning of a calling bout and it may be followed by a sequence of 0 to 6 B notes. We designed a playback experiment to mimick the effect of competing male calls with call bouts of different number of Bs on a naturally calling focal male. The A and B notes used in the playback tests were natural calls selected by their overall similarity with a sample of calls of different animals from the same population, measured through audiospectrogram correlations. Tests were performed in the field in southern Portugal with a set up that included an Apple portable computer and interactive playback 'Sound Maker' software (the call of the focal animal triggered the response of the playback sound). When exposed to stimuli with increasing number of B notes, males did not increase the number of B notes in their calls. They did increase call repetition rate. Other static call parameters (duration, frequency and number of pulses of A & B) did not change linearly with number of B notes in the stimulus.

21753: Year round radiotracking of Ambystoma maculatum, A. tigrinum, Cryptobranchus alleganiensis, and Rana clamitans has lead to improved package design, surgical procedures, field release and recovery, and positioning techniques. External packages are generally unacceptable for tracking amphibians. Amphibian skin is too physiologically active, delicate and moist for the attachment of external units by waist bands, harnesses, collars, glues or sutures. Packages fixed to the amphibian integument has caused tethering and even injury and death in the animal's struggle to free itself. External packages can also prevent amphibians from entering or turning around in small mammal tunnels, airways, vegetative tangles and rock crevices. External packages, stomach inserts, and surgical (coelomic) implants were used on aquatic hellbenders to test the various methods in a natural setting. The implants worked best, followed by the inserts, which were defecated after 10 days. External packages were unsatisfactory. Radiotransmitter implants were used successfully in all the above species, but precautions with design, implant surgery, and field deployment must be taken. Implant packages should be small enough to allow amphibians to turn around in tight spaces and be coated with beeswax instead of paraffin. Sutures should be more closely spaced in cold weather, and cyanoacrylate should be avoided. Animals should be released at the beginning of their daily activity cycle in the same pulse of ecological/social events from which they were removed. Finally, "local triangulation" should be used to obtain positions; visual fixes should normally be avoided.

21754: I carried out a laboratory study of foraging proficiency in young northern water snakes (Nerodia sipedon) presented with different water depths (0.25, 0.50, 1.00, 2.00 in.), and the presence or absence of artificial habitat structure. Over a seventeen month period and using two litters of young water snakes, I performed three laboratory experiments in which I measured the time required to capture and ingest live minnows in a small feeding arena during 30-minute trials. Snakes generally took less time to capture fish in shallower water than they did in deeper water. Ingestion times largely were unaffected by depth. Larger/older snakes took less time to capture fish than did smaller/young snakes, and larger snakes also captured more fish than did smaller snakes. In an experiment using one litter of young snakes, I found that capture and ingestion times generally were unaffected by the presence of one form of habitat structure, despite its importance as documented in other studies.

21755: Two species of the all-female, parthenogenetic Cnemidophorus laredoensis complex (Teiidae) coexist with the bisexual species Cnemidophorus gularis in the Rio Grande Valley of southern Texas and northern Mexico. I studied the behavior of the two parthenogenetic species, provisionally designated 'LAR-A' (= C. laredoensis) and 'LAR-B', and C. gularis through focal animal observations of free-ranging lizards in a state park in Texas. Focal animals were followed for a minimum of 10 minutes and all behaviors were recorded into a tape recorder. Playback of the tapes allowed determination of the amount of time lizards spent performing various behaviors. Observations were made during the May to June breeding seasons of 1994-1996. The major differences were between males of C. gularis and LAR-A, LAR-B, and C. gularis females. In general, C. gularis males spent a significantly greater percentage of time interacting with other lizards (most often courting conspecific females or parthenogenetic females), moved greater distances during the time they were observed, and moved faster than C. gularis females and females of the two parthenogenetic species. There were few behavioral differences between C. gularis females and parthenogenetic females. The two parthenogens did devote a greater percentage of their time to searching for food than did C. gularis males and females; however there was no significant difference in the rate of capture of arthropod prey. Overall, the results suggest that the behavioral differences between sexes are greater than the behavioral differences between species in this group of lizards despite differing reproductive modes.

21756: Spatial orientation is necessary for snake survival, mediating important behaviors such as den localization and predator escape responses. To characterize cues used for spatial orientation, eight juvenile corn snakes were trained to find the only open hole within a circular arena, given a choice of eight holes. During training, snakes showed significant decreases in the latency to find the goal and in the path length taken to find the goal. A significant increase was found in the percent movement in the goal quadrant. Manipulations of controlled environmental cues (rotation of a cue card, rotation of the arena, release from a new position in the arena, and removal of the cue card) were done to examine the effects on orientation to the goal. The results indicate that no one particular cue was used by all of the snakes, although rotation of the cue card and arena affected the most snakes. Individuals were affected differently by different cue manipulations, and some snakes appear to use multiple environmental cues for this task. Snakes also appear to use cues which were not manipulated, such as extra-arena (e.g. overhead lights) and intra-arena cues (e.g. variation in the arena surface).

21757: If predation is a serious threat to salamanders, and if predation is more likely when salamanders are moving about at night, away from a place of retreat, then it would seem an unnecessary risk for well fed salamanders to move about as much as those which are having difficulty finding food. Juvenile Plethodon glutinosus, measuring 35-50mm svl, of two feeding groups, 6 in each group, were kept in enclosures where nocturnal movements could be detected by infrared beam interruptions. Enclosures measured 35 x 35cm, were 5cm in height, and a single cover object was provided in the center of each. Small crickets, 6-10mm, were given as food every 5th day within the 20 days of recording. Well fed salamanders ate 4-6 crickets at a feeding and gained mass over the test period. The less well fed salamanders were allowed 1-2 crickets at a feeding and either gained or lost mass minimally. The well fed group demonstrated significantly less movement than the group which ate less (t=4.27, p<0.001). These results are consistent with a view that movements outside of a place of retreat pose a risk for juvenile P. glutinosus.

21758: Classic studies of gill vasculature indicate the gross anatomy of elasmobranch gills is similar in most species, and in general, resembles those of teleosts. Studies of fine gill structure of several species of batoid elasmobranchs have, however, reported some structural differences. These differences include the presence, in urolophids (Urolophus jamaicensis, U. mucosus, U. paucimaculatus), of 1) a tip channel, possibly an extension of the afferent filament artery that runs along the top of the filament corpus cavernosum, and 2) a vascular arcade, a vessel which connects the afferent filament arteries of a hemibranch near the tip of each filament. To date, these structures were believed to be unique to the urolophids as they were not found in either rajids (Raja erinacea, R. clavata) or the shark Scyliorhinus canicula. Research with the cownose ray (Rhinoptera bonasus) and other batoid elasmobranchs, however, indicates the tip channel and vascular arcade are not unique to urolophids. Additional research is required to determine the phylogenetic and physiologic significances of these structures.

21759: Hyla chrysoscelis, family Hylidae, ranges from Southern Canada south to Texas and Florida. Internal oral morphology and chondrocranial anatomy for this species have not been described. However, chondrocranial data is available for eight species within the family Hylidae. Herein, we describe the internal oral anatomy using scanning electron microscopy (SEM), chondrocranial anatomy, and ossification sequence for H. chrysoscelis. Specimens were field collected in Beaverdam, Virginia, and preserved in 10% formalin. A total of 43 tadpoles, ranging from Gosner's stages 30 to 46, were cleared and double-stained for bone and cartilage using standard techniques. A table of ossification sequence is presented. In addition, two tadpoles were prepared for SEM using standard techniques. Hyla chrysoscelis differs in several characteristics from the other described members of the family Hylidae. It is most similar to the previously described H. puchella and H. lanciformis. However, in H. chrysoscelis the anterior tips of the cornua trabeculae are laterally expanded. Hyla chrysoscelis has an otic process connecting the palatoquadrate to the otic capsule. This process was reported absent in H. lanciformis. The muscular process of H. chrysoscelis is smaller than that of H. pulchella. The internal oral anatomy of H. chrysoscelis is similar to that reported for other hylids.

21760: The chondrocranial morphology and skeletogenesis of tadpoles in the genus Physalaemus remains unknown. Herein, we describe the chondrocranial morphology of three species: Physalaemus gracilis, P. henselii, and P. pustulosus. Skeletogenesis is reported based on complete developmental series of P. gracilis and P. pustulosus. Tadpoles were fixed, staged (following Gosner's table, 1960), and cleared and double-stained for cartilage and bone using standard procedures. Examination of the whole-mounted and stained specimens revealed little difference in chondrocranial anatomy and the onset of ossification among the three species. Physalaemus is characterized by having suprarostrals in which the ala and the corpus are fused dorsally. Furthermore the suprarostrals are ventromedially fused. Physalaemus also exhibits a well-developed processus quadratoethmoidalis. A processus pseudopterygoideus is present only in P. gracilis. The processus antorbitalis fuses to the tip of the processus muscularis in P. pustulosus and P. henselii to form a commisura quadratoorbitalis, this connection is lacking in P. gracilis. The frontoparietal fenestra of P. pustulosus and P. gracilis is completely divided by well-developed taeni tectum transversalis and taeni tectum medialis, these taenia are absent in P. henselii. A larval otic process is absent and the processus ascendens has an intermediate attachment to the braincase in all three species

21761: The ethmoid plate of anuran larvae is formed by the fusion of the trabecular and parachordal cartilages early in development. From the antero-lateral edges of this plate, the cornua trabeculae arise as two separate and anteriorly diverging projections. Usually, at their most anterior tips, the cornua trabeculae articulate with the suprarostral cartilages, the element supporting the upper jaw. Modification of the cornua has been demonstrated in several taxa (Wild 1996). In pipids, cornua trabeculae and suprarostral cartilages are not identifiable as separate elements even in relatively early larvae (Nieuwkoop and Faber stage 50). Instead, a single and continuous cartilaginous plate covers the entire area, the suprarostral plate (Trueb and Hanken 1993). This plate has been reported in Xenopus, Pipa, and Rhinophrynus. Hymenochirus boettgeri lacks a suprarostral plate and possesses a further modified ethmoid area. Tadpoles of Xenopus laevis, Rhinophrynus dorsalis and Hymenochirus boettgeri were studied using whole-mounted cleared and stained specimens and paraffin and plastic embedded cross-sectioned material. Herein we describe the development of the suprarostral plate in Xenopus laevis, Rhinophrynus dorsalis with comments on the condition in Hymenochirus boettgeri

21762: Since Taylor's Atlas of Scales (1972), interspecific variation among caecilian scales has been virtually ignored, and only the presence or absence of scales has been used as a phylogenetic character. The issue of variation has focused on scale morphology within and among individuals of a single species. Considerable variation has been found in the size, shape, arrangement, and number of scales, and thus, scales have been regarded as too variable to be phylogenetically informative. The surface morphology of scales has been investigated in detail in only a few taxa. The outer-most layer of caecilian scales is comprised of mineralized squamulae. The objectives of this study were to investigate intraspecific and interspecific variation in the arrangement and shape of the squamulae, and to address whether there are scale characteristics, besides the presence or absence of scales, that can be utilized in reconstructing phylogenies. Scales from representative of the four caecilian families that possess scales were removed and analyzed using light and scanning electron microscopy. Little intraspecific variation was found in scale ultrastructure, while a good deal of interspecific variation was identified. Variation in scale ultrastructure among taxa is quantified and scale characters are discussed.

21763: During courtship, male ground skinks frequently bite the body of female lizards. 21764: The laterophysic connection is a unique mechanical linkage between anterior horns of the swim bladder and the lateral line canals in the post-temporal bones of the skull in fishes of the genus Chaetodon. Webb and Blum (1990) and Webb (in press) described this well-developed connection in C. octofasciatus and suggest that this connection may allow these fishes to detect pressure stimuli using their lateral line system. 21765: The development of the supraorbital and mandibular canals was analyzed in Archocentrus nigrofasciatus (n=26, 4.5-11.5 mm SL) in order to evaluate conflicting descriptions of canal morphogenesis and the manner in which they are incorporated into dermal cranial bones. Neuromasts of the dorsal aspect of the head were examined (n=6, 4.5 - 8.0 mm SL) using SEM to clarify their identity as presumptive canal or superficial neuromasts. Four developmental stages were identified. Neuromasts arise in the epithelium (Stage I) and a bony plate ossifies under each neuromast. Epithelial ridges arise on either side of the neuromast and ossify intramembranously forming canal walls (Stage II). The epithelium fuses over the neuromast (Stage III) and canal walls fuse medially (Stage IV) forming the lateral line canal roof. Thus, the supraorbital and mandibular canals appear to develop as outgrowths of the underlying dermal bone, not as separate ossifications. In addition, regression analyses reveal that neuromast width and canal width exhibit a positive linear relationship with fish size in both the supraorbital and mandibular canals indicating that there are probably ongoing interactions between neuromasts and dermal bones after initial canal ossification.

21768: Two populations of newly metamorphosed Northwestern salamanders were analyzed for population and cohort size. 21769: Myogenic heterochronies have not been studied in anurans. Xenopus laevis exhibits muscle function prior to multinucleation of axial myotome. It is interesting to determine if the early muscle function in X. laevis is a heterochronic event shared with other pipids or a unique trait of X. laevis. Herein, we studied myogenesis in the pipid Hymenochirus boettgeri. We specifically focused on the timing of four events: 1) initial presence of muscle protein, 2) first stimulated twitch, 3) first spontaneous twitch, and 4) onset of multinucleation. Muscle protein was detected at stage 25 (Nieuwkoop and Faber, 1956, developmental table for Xenopus) using the 12/101 anti-muscle antibody and the DAB substrate reaction. Muscle was stimulated with a metal probe and observations were made under a dissecting microscope. Stimulated first twitch took place by stages 27/28, whereas spontaneous twitch occurred at stage 31. Methacrylate sections stained with toluidine blue revealed multinucleated myotome after stage 42. Overall, myogenic events in H. boettgeri occur in the same sequence as in X. laevis, but delayed by 2-3 stages, except multinucleation, which occurs around the same stage in both species. In addition, first heartbeat is also delayed in H. boettgeri (stage 36/37, compared to 33/34 in X. laevis).

21770: Aroclor® 1242 is a polychlorinated biphenyl (PCB) formulation reported to have endocrine disrupting activity in many animals. In the second egg mass, tentatively identified as R. palustris, PCB treatment was correlated with an increase in the number of tadpoles completing metamorphosis, significantly in the highest dose. The apparent stimulation of metamorphosis in the second egg mass by PCB exposure may be due to an endocrine disrupting effect on the corticosterone "stress" axis. A thyroid-mediated mechanism of effect is also possible. The increase in metamorphosis in the PCB treated groups was only significant at the highest dose (1000 pg/g). This level of contamination exceeds concentrations likely to occur in the wild. Based upon these results, it is unlikely that PCB exposure in the wild is altering time to metamorphosis to a degree that would detrimentally effect amphibian populations. 21772: From June to October 1994, we used five drift fences, 20 m-long with 10 pitfall traps each side, to sample migrating red efts (Notophthalmus viridescens) in terrestrial habitats near Lake Lafond in the Mastigouche Reserve, Quebec. 21773: Changes in head size and shape during development occur in all vertebrates. One general observation is that the eyes of most vertebrates are large early in development and that the remainder of the head tends to grow around them. This paper presents a comparative study of the relative size and position of the eyes within and among different groups of snakes. Of particular interest are changes associated with head size in left and right visual field overlap, with respect to both quantity and direction of overlap. For example, in some arboreal species, the eyes are rotated about the dorsal-ventral axis towards the frontal plane during ontogeny. This increases the frontal binocular overlap, while sacrificing some of the postero-lateral visual field. These changes may be the consequence of structural changes to increase gape and the development of larger, more powerful jaw musculature in larger individuals for capturing and ingesting larger prey. Correlations with natural history and phylogeny are discussed together with some hypotheses of ultimate causation.

21775: The lake chub (Couesius plumbeus), the most widespread minnow in northern North America, ranges from Alaska to New England. 21776: Surface fresh waters represent 0.01% of the planet's water, of which 1% was in rivers, 99% in lakes. Now reservoirs hold five times as much water as river beds and affect flow seasonality. Agriculture severely affects fish habitat by water withdrawal and quality of runoff. Biological (exotics) and industrial chemical pollution also affect ecosystem integrity. Freshwater fishes comprise 40.4% of the world's fish species. Freshwater fish diversity is unevenly distributed. Polar and arid areas have few species, rivers more than lakes. Six countries, Brazil, Indonesia, China, Zaire, Peru and U.S., contain over 90% of freshwater fish species. Species geographic density, rather than absolute counts, provides a different country list. Equal-area geographic grids offer a superior method of identifying biodiversity hotspots. Globally about 20% of the world's freshwater fish species are extinct, endangered, or vulnerable. Numerous productive fisheries are at risk. Driving forces, not just immediate human impacts need to be considered. 54% of the planet's accessible runoff is now used in growing human populations. Present economic frameworks are reducing capacity of governments to respond. Serious responses need to be initiated before the new millennium if the collision between needs of humans and freshwater biota does not result in massive extinctions.

21777: A distinctive form of longnose sucker, the Salish sucker, occurs in southwestern British Columbia and western Washington. Salish suckers differ from other western longnose suckers in both their morphometry and mitochondrial genome. Thus, both morphometric and molecular data indicate that Salish suckers have diverged from other northwestern longnose suckers; however, our molecular data suggests an even 'deeper' divergence between western and eastern longnose suckers, and the Salish sucker is unambiguously part of the western lineage. This implies that the Salish sucker evolved after the divergence of western and eastern longnose suckers. The geographic distribution of Salish suckers is consistent with a pre-Wisconscinan origin south of Puget Sound and post glacial dispersal north into southwestern B.C. The Salish sucker is in decline throughout its geographic range and probably will be extinct in southwestern B.C. within a decade. The diagnostic mitochondrial haplotypes characteristics of the Salish sucker argue that a unique part of the evolutionary history of the longnose sucker will be lost with the extinction of the Salish sucker. As such they constitute and Evolutionarily Significant Unit and warrant some protection in Washington State where there still is at least one large population.

21778: Muskellunge, the largest freshwater sports species in temperate North America, are venerable fish whose size and stature match those of their benefactor, Dr. E. J. Crossman. 21779: In his direction to students, Dr. E.J. Crossman emphasizes and encourages a comprehensive approach to questions and problems of fish systematic and taxonomic studies which, at the time I was doing my degree work, were dominated by morphological and osetological approaches. Recently such studies have become dominated by genetic approaches which often rely solely upon tissues provided to laboratories rather than the fish themselves, and focus solely upon variation at the molecular level. Little or no reference is usually made to other character systems such as morphology, osteology, ecology or biology. For well known groups and studies at higher taxonomic levels this bias may not matter, and genetic studies add another dimension to our knowledge. However, for poorly known groups and lower taxonomic levels, working solely with tissues can limit understanding, may bias results, and result in erroneous conclusions. External morphology is often the first clue to undiscovered diversity. Genetic variation may be present but without associated knowledge of morphology may not be interpreted correctly. Thus, quantifying and understanding morphological diversity is important in the development of hypotheses which can then be tested using other approaches such as genetics. Morphological diversity within an esociform (Olympic mudminnow, Novumbra hubbsi) and morphological and genetic diversity within a salmoniform group (Arctic and Dolly Varden chars, Salvelinus spp.) are used to illustrate the need for close association of various approaches to achieve fuller understanding of diversity and relationships of fishes. In keeping with the legacy of Dr. Crossman, I advocate a more comprehensive approach to systematic and taxonomic studies which should include reference to morphological, ecological and biological chararactes as well as genetic characters.

21780: We quantified individual differences in reproductive behaviour of Atlantic cod under simulated natural conditions. 21783: The need for better understanding of the changes in the biodiversity of the fishes of the Great Lakes includes the need to inventory the number of fishes introduced and those which become extirpated. 21786: In 1976 James Huheey used a functional feeding model to simulate the effects of adding weaker models to simple Mullerian Mimicry system. I used a similar functional model of feeding to ask whether specific changes alter the conclusion that Mullerian Mimicry cannot exist. 21805: Although many studies have ascribed potential benefits of increased water availability during incubation to neonatal survival in turtles, none have directly examined how differential water availability influences the migratory behavior of the hatchlings under field conditions. 21820: The role of nest-site choice in the population biology of species with temperature-dependent sex determination (TSD) is virtually unexplored despite its importance in theoretical models for the evolution of sex ratio in such species. 21821: For the last decade, interest in modeling chelonian growth has increased and provided a framework for better understanding of this life history trait. 21842: Phoxinus eos-neogaeus are all-female fish from the northern United States and southern Canada that reproduce by gynogenesis, a form of clonal reproduction. These fish were formed by hybridization between a female of Phoxinus neogaeus and a male of Phoxinus eos; they express one enzyme allele (allozyme) of P. eos and one allozyme of P. neogaeus for each enzyme for which the parental allozymes can be distinguished by cellulose acetate electrophoresis. We have analyzed the expression of phosphoglucomutase (PGM) and glucosephosphate isomerase (GPI) in heart, eye, muscle, and liver of ten or more diploid and triploid individuals (with 5-7 replicates of each individual) of P. eos-neogaeus. Although a one:one ratio of expression is expected in diploid individuals, the expression of the P. eos allele is statistically significantly greater than the P. neogaeus allele in some tissues for PGM, and in other tissues for GPI. In triploid individuals, expression of the P. eos allozyme for GPI is expressed significantly less than expected. These data indicate a difference in the regulation of the parental allozymes by tissue and enzyme that may effect the ecological role of the hybrid species, and may explain how polyploids survive with three sets of chromosomes directing their cellular activities.

21843: Multicolor fluorescence in situ hybridization (M-FISH) is a new technique which allows localization of multiple DNA probes on chromosomes from a single metaphase. We have used this technique to localize different families of repetitive sequences to the chromosomes of zebrafish (Danio rerio) and several species of salmonid fishes including rainbow trout (Oncorhynchus mykiss) and lake trout (Salvelinus namaycush). Chromosome preparations were obtained from a diploid cell line of zebrafish and from cultured blood of the salmonid species. Cloned probes were labeled with either Spectrum Orange or Spectrum Green using the polymerase chain reaction (PCR) and slides were counterstained with DAPI. Images were captured with a CCD camera and analyzed with QUIPS software (Vysis, Inc.). Different families and sub-families of repetitive DNAs were localized at different centromeric, subcentromeric, and subtelomeric locations in each species. These probes will be useful for identification of fish chromosomes in gene localization experiments using M-FISH.

21844: My research concerns the conservation of quantitative trait loci (QTL) coding for the quantitative trait of upper thermal tolerance (UTT) (resistance time in the zone of maximal thermal stress) in commercial rainbow trout (Oncorhynchus mykiss) populations. Previous research indicates the existence of four major QTL for UTT segregating in inbred lines selected for response to this trait. Individuals used in this study are the result of intra- and interstrain cross progeny of two unselected strains of commercial rainbow trout. Parental fish were derived from the combination of two grandsires and 12 grandams within each strain. Preliminary analysis indicates that major allelic variants are segregating in these hatchery strains for the previously identified UTT QTL. The ongoing survey of this progeny generation may reveal additional QTL allelic variants. Later work will attempt to determine the physiological mechanism by which the marked quantitative trait loci contribute to the total phenotype by assessing linkage between candidate coding loci (e.g. heat-shock proteins [hsps]) and variation in neutral microsatellite markers. The discovery of QTL-associated variance for this trait in strains unselected for UTT suggests that QTL variants for upper temperature tolerance may be fairly widespread in natural populations of rainbow trout.

21845: It has been proposed that population structure of aquatic organisms is determined by the number of environmental settings allowing completion of their life cycles. In this study, we test the hypothesis that this leads to the development of within-river population structuring associated with the existing number of spawning/nursery areas in anadromous Atlantic salmon. A total of 700 alevins sampled shortly after emergence (50 fish x 7 sites x 2 years) were genotyped using five microsatellite loci. Heterogeneity in allele frequency distribution, translating into significant Fst values among all pairwise comparisons of sites were observed for the two consecutive years of sampling. These parameters were lower among inter-annual samples of a same site than among sites. The majority of samples also clustered by sites in a neighbor-joining tree built from chord-distance. These results therefore support the hypothesis that genetic population substructuring in Atlantic salmon may develop at a very small geographic scale, as a consequence of the existing number of grounds favoring survival of young life-history stages. Because salmon associated with such population subunits may develop local adaptations, conservation and management policies should be planned to preserve their genetic integrity.

21846: The red snapper (Lutjanus campechanus) is one of the most economically-important fishes in the Gulf of Mexico (Gulf). Previous analyses of mitochondrial (mt) DNA in the northern Gulf detected no significant differences in haplotype frequency across a geographic gradient and no partitioning of uncommon haplotypes, indicating that red snappers in the northern Gulf comprise a single genetic population. However, differences in mtDNA haplotype diversity among several samples indicated that some level of genetic population structure exists, and that perhaps a more rapidly-evolving genetic character might reveal that structure. We therefore developed a suite of highly polymorphic DNA microsatellite loci to further examine the partitioning of genetic variation in this species. A subgenomic library of restriction fragments was screened with di-, tri-, and tetra-nucleotide repeat and several microsatellite loci were identified and sequenced. Oligonucleotide primers for amplification of loci via polymerase chain reaction were developed. Polymorphism in microsatellite allele size was scored on denaturing polyacrylamide gels. Microsatellite allele frequencies from different year classes and different regions were compared to further test the hypothesis that red snapper from the northern Gulf comprise a single genetic population.

21847: While reduction and loss of external limbs are hallmarks of amphisbaenian evolution, internal girdle and hindlimb remnants in some amphisbaenian taxa have been known for many years. However, less than half of the known genera have been surveyed for internal remnants of the appendicular skeleton and these structures have not been systematically compared. I surveyed the appendicular skeleton in all extant genera of amphisbaenians via the preparation and study of radiographs, dry skeletons, and cleared and stained specimens and compared them to each other as well as to other non- and reduced-limbed squamates. This study revealed that relative reduction of girdle and limb elements is diverse among the group. Variability in bony and cartilagenous components of the girdle and limb remnants appears to contain useful information for ongoing phylogenetic studies of amphisbaenian interrelationships. All amphisbaenians retain at least one bony pelvic element but many amphisbaenians have completely lost the pectoral girdle. Among squamates, regardless of the degree of limb reduction or loss, the pelvic girdle never completely disappears in amphisbaenians or 'lizards' as it does in most snakes, and the pectoral girdle never completely disappears in 'lizards' as it does in many amphisbaenians and all snakes.

21848: The genus Liolaemus (Iguania: Tropiduridae) is the largest genus of lizards in the Southern Hemisphere. Partially as a consequence of this diversity, the intrageneric relationships within Liolaemus are largely enigmatic. Approximately half of the nearly 170 described taxa in the genus belong to the chiliensis group. Within this large clade, several species groups have been informally recognized including the alticolor and the elongatus groups. I undertook an analysis of mitochondrial DNA to ascertain the relationships among members of the alticolor and elongatus species groups to (1) determine if members of each of these species groups formed monophyletic lineages; and (2) address the evolution of viviparity within these groups. I sequenced about 700 bp (167 informative) of the mitochondrial 12S gene for nearly all described and several undescribed species within the two species groups. A maximum parsimony analysis recovered three equally parsimonious trees. A consensus tree of the mtDNA results were then combined with additional evidence derived from morphological and ecological studies. The combined phylogenetic hypothesis suggests that the two groups are indeed monophyletic. Furthermore, viviparity appears to have evolved independently several times within the alticolor group, but only once for the elongatus group, wherein, one species may have reverted to oviparous reproduction.

21849: The amount of genetic variability present may indicate a species' ability to adapt to a stressful environment and can be examined in a quantitative genetic analysis. Currently, numerous conservation efforts are being devoted to determining whether amphibian species are in decline, as many studies would suggest. Therefore, because amphibians are amenable to quantitative genetic analyses and because their numbers may be declining due to changes in their environment, these organisms serve as an excellent model for examining the relationship between the amount of genetic variability present in populations and adaptability in changing environments. Using tadpoles of a single southern leopard frog (Rana sphenocephala) population, I examined the amount of genetic variability among full- and half-sib families with respect to their sensitivity to both lethal (time-to-death) and sublethal (changes in activity) levels of the agricultural chemical, carbaryl. Analyses of both time-to-death and activity data indicate significant differences among full sib families, suggesting a great deal of variability, genetic or environmental, present in the responses to this environmental stressor. There were also significant differences among half sib families in the degree to which activity was reduced by sublethal carbaryl levels, indicating that this variability has a genetic basis.

21850: The Mojave fringe-toed lizard, Uma scoparia, is restricted to sand dunes in the Mojave Desert, existing in 25 known localities. Because of this species' restriction to sand dunes, it has been considered a species of special concern. Many populations are on the decline due to habitat destruction, misuse of off-road vehicles and possibly a significant increase in raven numbers. The determination of the extent and geographic distribution of genetic diversity among the Mojave fringe-toed lizards is imperative for conservation and potential augmentation of endangered populations. Augmentation of the Fort Irwin population is essential due to the rapidly declining population size, which is critical since small populations are highly susceptible to stochastic events. If this population is to remain reproductively viable, then genetic viability and integrity, including local adaptations must be maintained by introducing 'sister' populations; individuals from populations that are most similar genetically. The mitochondrial genes ATPase 6 and cytochrome b were sequenced for 27 U. scoparia from 8 localities, using U. notata as outgroup. In total, 1676 combined base pairs were sequenced, of which 170 were potentially phylogenetically informative. Results of parsimony analysis revealed that the most closely related populations to NTC Fort Irwin are the dunes at Kelso and Pisgah Crater, located southeast of the base.

21851: A phylogeny of the family Lacertidae was derived from mtDNA gene sequence data. Thirty-two species, representing 22 currently recognized genera and subgenera, were included in the analysis. A total of 3,600 base pairs was obtained and aligned from 12S, 16S and COI gene sequences. A preferred tree was selected based on weighted parsimony and functional ingroup and outgroup analyses. Decay analysis, bootstrap and permutation tail probability were used to evaluate support for the recovered nodes. The genus Gallotia was resolved as the basal taxon and the sister group of all remaining lacertids. Takydromus branched off next. All African lacertids grouped together, and formed a monophyletic clade with the Eurasian genera Eremias and Ophisops. The remaining Eurasian lacertids sequentially branched off near the base of the tree in a 'comb-like' fashion. The basal position of Gallotia and the monophyly of African lacertids are consistent with previous hypotheses. The European-origin hypothesis of lacertids is favored, and the distribution of lacertids in Africa is likely a dispersal event.

21852: The zygosphene-zygantrum articulations of snake vertebrae are hypothesized to restrict or eliminate vertebral torsion. This hypothesis is apparently based solely on the inference of function from structure, despite contradictory evidence. Gasc (1974, Mem. Mus. Nat. Hist. Nat., Paris Ser. A Zool. 83:1-182) measured vertebral torsion of 1-2°/joint in dried Python skeletons, but his results are seldom cited. I observed axial torsion during lateral undulation and feeding in Pituophis melanoleucus. To determine whether apparent axial torsion results from differential movement of the left and right body walls, combined lateral and vertical bending, or actual torsion at the vertebral joints, I examined close-up video images of crawling P. melanoleucus and digitized macro video images of torsion in fresh sections of the trunk. To measure vertebral torsion, I clamped sections of 10 vertebrae at one end and twisted the free end by hand; the limits of twisting were clearly detectable and were reached before the movement produced any axial bending. Freely crawling P. melanoleucus exhibited negligible lifting, moderate differential movement of the left and right body walls, and apparent torsion of 0.02-2.4°/vertebra. Fresh trunk sections allowed actual torsion of 0.3-1.1°/vertebra, which produced substantial overall torsion when added over several vertebrae. Therefore, the observed torsion was likely produced by differential movement of the left and right body walls combined with real torsion at the vertebral joints. Despite the mechanical restrictions imposed by the complex articulations, vertebral torsion occurs in snakes and appears to be functionally important in many kinds of snake movements.

21853: Widespread use of agricultural chemicals makes it increasingly likely that non-target wildlife could be exposed to contamination. Many amphibian species utilize breeding habitats nested within or around agricultural areas, therefore population and community dynamics may be influenced or altered by exposure to chemicals. The chemical used in this experiment, carbaryl, is the active ingredient in the insecticide Sevin. This chemical acts through acetylcholinesterase inhibition, and is known to affect amphibian activity and behavior. The objectives of this experiment were to determine differential susceptibility to carbaryl among species, the effect of the chemical under different biotic conditions, and the indirect effects of the chemical. To do this, I used three species of anurans in outdoor cattle tanks: Hyla versicolor (gray treefrog), Bufo woodhousii (toad) and Rana clamitans (green frog). Twelve experimental treatments were manipulated for density (high or low), predator (presence or absence of Notophthalmus viridescens) and chemical level (0, 3.5, or 7.0 mg/l of carbaryl). Results showed that the chemical significantly affected size at metamorphosis in H. versicolor. A predator by chemical effect in H. versicolor was significant; in the presence of the predator, tadpoles at high chemical levels had a larger size at metamorphosis than other classes. Chemical effects on survival at metamorphosis were significant in B. woodhousii and H. versicolor; higher chemical levels significantly reduced survival. The chemical interacts with biotic factors in ways that would not be predictable from two-factor experiments. Chemical by density interactions were significant in B. woodhousii and H. versicolor. This experiment does indicate differential susceptibility among species and noted that differences in biotic conditions affect the potency of the chemical.

21854: In order to determine biogeographic relationships, Parsimony Analysis of Endemicity (PAE) was applied to presence/absence of species of anurans in 14 localities of lowland Neotropical rainforests in the Chocoan Region, Central America, Amazon Basin, and Brazilian Atlantic Forest. Phylogenetic Analysis Using Parsimony (PAUP 3.1) of 340 species led to two most parsimonious area cladograms (TL = 475, CI = 0.705). The strict consensus showed a basal polytomy among three regions: (1) Central America and Choco, (2) Amazon Basin, and (3) Atlantic Forest. Within the Amazon Basin, the localities in the Upper Amazonian in Peru and Ecuador were separated from those in the Lower Amazon Basin (Guianan Region + Belem). A PAE of presence/absence of 108 lizard species in 13 areas in Central America and the Amazon Basin led to a single most parsimonious area cladogram (TL = 156, CI = 0.692). The Central American localities were separated from those of the Amazon Basin. Within the Amazon Basin, a separation between Upper Amazonian in Ecuador and Peru and Lower Amazonian was observed. This pattern is similar to the pattern obtained from the anuran PAE.

21855: A major focus for contemporary studies of natural hybridization is experimental determination of the relative fitness of parental and hybrid genotypes and measurements of the interactions between the genotype and environment. Natural hybridization occurs between two anuran species, Rana blairi and Rana sphenocephala. To determine the relative fitness of parental and hybrid genotypes in sympatric leopard frog populations in Missouri, I examined the performance of parental and hybrid larvae to measure differences in viability. Artificial crosses between R. blairi and R. sphenocephala produced two parental and three hybrid genotypes. Resultant larvae were reared in experimental ponds in single- and mixed-genotype populations. Analyses of variance indicated that R. sphenocephala decreased its larval period length when reared with F1 backcross hybrid larvae relative to when reared alone. F1 backcross hybrid ponds produced more metamorphs when larvae were reared with either parental species relative to when reared alone. When reared together, both R. sphenocephala and F1 hybrids metamorphosed at larger body masses than when reared separately. These results indicate that parental and hybrid genotypes perform at equivalent or higher levels when reared together compared to single-genotype ponds. Such evidence suggests that larval dynamics may play an important role in maintaining the coexistence of genotypes in this hybrid zone.

21856: Remarkable morphological similarity among the cascade (waterfall) ranids of southeast Asia has made them a taxonomic bane for 160 years. Central among this confusion has been the green cascade frog, Rana livida. Inhabiting the fast moving mountain rivers and forests of Indochina, this stink frog has long been suspected of being composed of several species. Recently collected specimens from Vietnam keyed out to R. livida, but exhibited evident morphological differences across populations. A combination of morphology, morphometrics, DNA content analysis, and allozyme electrophoresis was used to investigate whether or not any of these morphotypes were distinct species. The results from this investigation suggested the presence of 5 distinct species. A phylogeny for the group using partial mitochondrial 16S gene sequences was estimated. A 537 base pair region yielded 91 potentially informative characters. Maximum parsimony was used to evaluate the data. Because these species were identified over a very small portion of the geographic range of the Rana livida group, it is expected that this phylogeny will be expanded as more species of this poorly understood complex are discovered.

21857: Deserts are characterized by extreme environmental and resource variation; many desert reptiles have the ability to tolerate these stresses through behavioral and physiological mechanisms. Desert horned lizards, Phrynosoma platyrhinos, are one of the most common lizards in the Mojave desert. Horned lizards are morphologically adapted to exploit ants as their primary food source, and they are characterized by certain aspects of typical sit-and-wait predators. It has been suggested that desert horned lizards should have relatively low energy requirements because of their foraging strategy and because they inhabit an area typified by low resource availability. To address this hypothesis, I used doubly labeled water to measure the energy and water turnover of a population of desert horned lizards over a five year study period. The annual rainfall of the study area varied during the study period such that there were normal, very wet and very dry conditions. This allowed me to examine the physiological plasticity of horned lizards. The results of my research will be presented.

21858: This study contributes to the knowledge of Amazonian herpetology by evaluating the mensurable and meristic characters associated with ontogeny, sexual dimorphism, and geographic variation of the Amazonian tree frog Hyla geographica. The taxonomic significance of the displayed variations was analyzed by evaluating external characters. Four hundred eleven specimens from the following museums were examined: Museum of Comparative Zoology at Harvard, U.S. National Museum of Natural History, and Chicago Museum of Natural History. This analysis included population samples from the following political entities: Trinidad, Colombia, French Guiana, Guyana, Suriname, Ecuador, Bolivia, Peru, and Brazil. Mensurable characters obtained were: head-length (HL), head-width (HW), tympanum-diameter (TD), femur-length (FL), and snout-vent-length (SVL). These measurements were used to calculate morphology ratios for analysis of ontogenetic growth variations. The means, standard deviation, and range of all mensurable characters and growth ratios were determined. Distribution patterns of pigments were coded and recorded for all specimens. The pigment patterns, or absence of pigments were recorded for the snout, venter, dorsum, thigh, flank, upper arm, and dorsal aspect of the head. All specimens were examined for sexual maturity. The variations of the mensurable characters, morphological ratios, and patterns of pigment distribution suggest that the populations of H. geographica do not display significant geoclines and, therefore, are one widely distributed species.

21859: Thamnophis sirtalis is a widely distributed, highly variable, snake which is common throughout much of its North American range. Historically, this species has been subdivided into many subspecies based predominantly on geographical variation in colour pattern, although there is also variation in life history traits and meristic characters. Of the twelve currently recognized subspecies, several meet in broad areas of intergradation which are forms of hybrid zones where there is introgression between distinct gene pools. In order to infer the evolutionary relationship of snakes on either side of these hybrid zones, a mitochondrial DNA gene genealogy was constructed. Cytochrome b was amplified from over 123 snakes representing most of the entire range. A 385 or 780 bp portion was sequenced on a ABI automated sequencer at the GenAlyTic facility at the University of Guelph and yielded 45 distinct haplotypes with 73 phylogenetically informative characters. The heuristic search option of Paup was used to find all equally most parsimonious trees (320 trees, length 126 steps, CI=0.71, RI=0.92, RC=0.65). The resulting strict consensus tree revealed three distinct clades whose geographical distributions are not concordant with those of currently recognized subspecies.

21860: Despite the abundance of studies of genetic diversity in freshwater fishes, few of them specifically addressed the role of habitat structure in partitioning genetic variance within and among populations. Microsatellite loci have recently been developed for Salvelinus fontinalis (Angers et al., 1995) and successfully used to assess population structure within the species. In this study, we analyzed the variability of six microsatellite loci among 25 brook charr populations samples (n=30) in order to correlate hydrographic structure with genetic organization. These populations originate from three Canadian National parks (Kouchibouguac, Fundy and Forillon), showing contrasting hydrographic structure. Considering the general characteristics of these habitats, we formulated the hypothesis that the ratio of interpopulation/intrapopulation genetic diversity will be inversely correlated with the potential for gene flow imposed by those systems. Results obtained supported our working hypotheses. Thus, the hierarchical analysis of molecular variance revealed that the lower ratio of interpopulation/intrapopulation genetic diversity was found in Kouchibouguac (high migration potential) [0.0703, P=0.01210] whereas an intermediate value was observed in Fundy (intermediate migration potential) [0.1771, P=0.00000]. The highest ratio was observed in Forillon (low migration potential) [1.6885, P=0.00000]. We discuss the importance of habitat complexity on genetic structure in the context of management and conservation.

21861: The identification of brook charr conservation units and processes responsible for their evolution are prerequisites to the conservation and management of the species in national parks. In this study we documented genetic diversity among brook charr populations from la Mauricie national park and investigated factors that can account for the variation observed. Thirty-six populations (n=30) from eight different drainages were genetically characterized at five microsatellites and mtDNA. The mtDNA homogeneity indicated a common refugial origin of all populations. In contrast, extensive polymorphism was observed at microsatellites. Eleven evolutionary lineages were identified and their divergence apparently predated the postglacial recolonization of the park, suggesting that the park was recolonized by multiple population waves from a single yet fragmented glacial refuge. Multivariate statistical analysis highlighted the role of hydrographic systems, altitude, and stocking as the main explanatory factors for the observed genetic structure. Altogether, these results suggest that the use of microsatellites may reorient our views about problems of temporal and geographical scales considered in conservation genetics.

21862: We reanalyzed the data of a recently published study of higher-level snake relationships, which was based on a UPGMA analysis of alleles at four "slowly-evolving" protein-coding loci. The distance matrix derived from these data contains a large number of ties, which are not explicitly revealed in many UPGMA programs. Our analyses of these data reveal that the single, well-resolved phenogram presented in the published study is only one among at least 9,999 equivalent UPGMA phenograms supported by the data, the consensus of which is largely unresolved. Additive distance analysis and character-based parsimony analysis of the same data yield even less resolution. Thus, regardless of one's preference regarding analytical approaches, the data in question are highly ambiguous concerning higher-level snake phylogeny. The highly resolved tree presented in the published study is an analytical artifact that was obtained only because the analysis failed to consider equivalent trees resulting from ties in the distance matrix.

21863: Microsatellite variation was surveyed in six populations of lean lake trout and two populations of siscowet lake trout from Lake Superior using heterologous primer pairs developed for brook trout (Salvelinus fontinalis) and Atlantic salmon (Salmo salar). 21864: The dolphin, Coryphaena hippurus, is a fast swimming, migratory, pelagic fish that supports important commercial and recreational fisheries throughout the tropical and subtropical waters of the world. Oxenford and Hunte (1986) suggested two distinct stocks exist in the western central Atlantic. The southern stock migrates from Grenada northwards to the Virgin Islands and then returns southeastwards in the Atlantic. The northern stock migrates from Puerto Rico northwards to North Carolina and returns via Bermuda. The purpose of my study is to test Oxenford and Hunte's (1986) two stock hypothesis and investigate the possible presence of additional stocks using mitochondrial DNA analysis. Dolphin samples were obtained throughout their range in the western central Atlantic, Gulf of Mexico, and Caribbean by port sampling and attending offshore fishing tournaments. Preliminary results from restriction fragment length polymorphisms of the ND-1 region of the mitochondrial genome will be reviewed. Significant genetic differences between geographic localities provides strong evidence of demographic isolation and indicates the need for independent management of individual stocks (Dixon 1992, Moritz 1994). In August 1997, the South Atlantic Fishery Management Council proposed management options for the highly migratory dolphin fishery. Data provided by this study on the stock identification of the dolphin should be beneficial to the management of this fishery throughout the western Atlantic, Gulf of Mexico, and Caribbean.

21865: Fundulus heteroclitus is an abundant estuarine fish found along the Atlantic and Gulf coasts of the United States. This species has been the subject of numerous investigations of its own biology and has been used as a tool to study xenobiotic metabolism, development, and ecology. Hybrids between Fundulus heteroclitus and F. diaphanus from Nova Scotia reproduce clonally, and thus all individuals are genetically identical. Heterozygosity at codominantly expressed enzyme loci is detectable for all enzymes for which the parental species differ, with the exception of isocitrate dehydrogenase for which the F. diaphanus is not expressed. We have amplified the cytochrome b gene from the mitochondrial genome and cut it with restriction enzymes for which the two parental species have distinct restriction patterns to determine if the lack of expression of the F. diaphanus IDH allele is due to inactivation of a paternal allele, a phenomenon occasionally observed in hybrids. The hybrids share the restriction patterns of F. diaphanus, indicating that F. diaphanus is the maternal parent of the hybrid lineage. Lack of expression of the F. diaphanus allele must therefore be due to a mutation that inactivated this allele or another rare event.

21866: RAPD markers are powerful tools in the analysis of genetic relationships and genetic diversity. Recently, however, questions have risen concerning the inheritance patterns and the reproducibility of the RAPD markers. In this study, fragments generated by RAPD primers were tested for Mendelian inheritance in sailfin mollies. Mollies were collected from three locations in Florida, and over 25 single-pair matings of parents with known RAPD genotypes were made. Progeny from each mating were used to test patterns of inheritance. Of the sixty RAPD primers initially screened, 18 amplified polymorphic bands and two showed no variation. Repeatable, identical bands were amplified from both fin clips and muscle samples providing a mechanism for non-destructive genotyping of laboratory fish. 21867: Amphibians have been widely used as model systems for studying the early embryonic development of vertebrates. Although much of the early development of all amphibians is very similar, frogs and salamanders differ strikingly in the way they determine the germ cell lineage (the cells that will form eggs and sperm). The pattern observed in frogs is quite different than the one seen in other vertebrates; the salamander mechanism is apparently much more similar to that of birds and mammals. Although the pattern of germ cell formation has been elucidated in a wide variety of species, little is known about the genes governing this process. 21897: Other than anecdotal information obtained from commercial turtle trappers, relatively little data relating to the alligator snapping turtle (Macroclemys temminckii) in Georgia are available. 21898: Habitat segregation among related species has many ecological implications. However, the degree of spatial distribution differences in regions of sympatry is not well known for amphibians. 21899: Concerns over population declines and reports of malformations have led many agencies to become interested in inventory and monitoring of amphibians, especially frogs. Most of these programs rely primarily on calling surveys. Volunteers are often used in these efforts, and they are not necessarily trained herpetologists. For two years, my survey teams have conducted surveys of several species in a variety of habitats in western South Dakota. We have found that calling surveys are not necessarily the best census method for all anurans, and they may result in misleading conclusions. For federal lands in western South Dakota, we recommend calling surveys to monitor only one species, the chorus frog (Pseudacris triseriata). For most other species, calling surveys give misleading results or their success may depend on detailed knowledge of anuran life histories. Species which breed at temporary wetlands are easily overlooked when calling survey routes are designed. Calling behavior also appears to depend on certain climatic factors which have yet to be fully understood. 21900: Home range analyses are commonly used by herpetologists to test aspects of behaviour, demographics, reproductive strategies, and other aspects of ecology. Unfortunately, herpetologists (and other ecologists) often do not use the same rigorous standards when analyzing home ranges that they use for other statistical procedures. Home ranges are frequently estimated using different sample sizes, time intervals among observations, and total sampling periods, either among animals or among treatments. Using simulations and radiotelemetry data from snapping turtles (Chelydra serpentina), I demonstrate that home range estimates are dependent upon these three aspects of the sampling regime. In order to adequately test for treatment effects, home ranges must be analyzed using similar sample sizes and time intervals. Ironically, one aspect of home range analysis which ecologists have attempted to improve is autocorrelation. Traditionally, autocorrelation is believed to violate the assumptions of home range estimates, and so ecologists often subsample observations to reduce autocorrelation. However, I demonstrate that the accuracy and precision of home range estimates may improve with increasing autocorrelation, and reducing autocorrelation may cause more problems than it solves.

21901: We studied a population of common musk turtles (Sternotherus odoratus) in Georgian Bay, Ontario. These turtles occupy the shallow shoreline waters of the many small islands in this region. Animals occupying fragmented habitat appear to have larger home ranges relative to those that do not because unused space between and around fragments are included in the analysis. Two home range estimators, minimum convex polygon and harmonic mean, tend to overestimate home range in fragmented habitat. Cluster analysis is an estimator which reduces the amount of unused area within the estimate. Using radio-location data from the musk turtles we compared the accuracy of these three home range estimators. Cluster analysis was only more accurate than the harmonic mean estimator. However, the variability in accuracy was considerably less for cluster analysis relative to minimum convex polygon. We concluded that cluster analysis is a more appropriate home range estimator for animals in fragmented habitat than the minimum convex polygon or harmonic mean estimators.

21902: Game theory has greatly improved our understanding of animal behaviour, and can be used to predict the outcomes of fights or contests between individuals. This theory predicts that an animal's role might be used as a cue for contest settlement, thus reducing the cost of contests. The number of times that each turtle acquired a food item as well as the frequency of two aggressive behaviours, biting and mounting, were recorded. The results indicate that absolute body size, body size ratio between competitors and relatedness of individuals are not important determinants in the outcomes of contests or the frequency of aggression. 21903: Theory predicts that in polygynous species males should disperse from natal sites more than females because dispersal will promote the ability of males to compete for mates. 21905: Spotted turtles (Clemmys guttata) are listed as "Vulnerable" in Canada, and are similarly listed throughout the eastern U.S. Not much is known about hibernation in this species, therefore information on site fidelity and communal hibernaculum use may be important to the creation of conservation programs. 21909: During the course of field work over a 10-year period with the arboreal boa Corallus grenadensis on the West Indian island of Grenada, locals (e.g., farmers, forestry officials) invariably informed us that tree boas were not as common as they had been in the past. 21910: We investigated the role of underground refugia in the ecology of Heloderma suspectum, which spends over 95% of its time in shelters. 21911: The relationship between the spatial distribution of turtle nest sites and nest predation was investigated in a landscape encompassing a 12-ha freshwater wetland in west-central South Carolina. Nests were monitored from the day of oviposition until they were deemed to have successfully produced hatchlings or depredation was documented. The three-year mean predation rate was 84.2% (80%, 88%, and 81% for 1992, 1993 and 1994, respectively). Modeling of the point pattern of nest locations suggests that nests were distributed at varying densities. Logistic and autologistic regressions provided no evidence indicating that nest survival is dependent on the survivorship of neighboring nests. 21912: Mangrove communities are important habitats for fishes, yet significant extents of mangrove shorelines are being replaced by seawalls. 21913: Data and observations from recent studies of hard corals and algae indicate that lagoonal patch reefs have undergone a major change in their ecology associated with the 99% loss in the cover of branching corals (Acropora cervicornis and A. palmata), a 75% reduction in hard coral, and a 315% increase in erect brown algae (Lobophora, Dictyota, Turbinaria and Sargassum). 21916: Recent research has suggested that the dynamics of fish populations and assemblages within habitats can be affected by the spatial distribution (i.e., isolation) of these habitats within streams. In this study, we determined the extent to which pool isolation (determined by the distance between adjacent pools) influenced fish movement and assemblage dynamics in two Arkansas streams. We marked common species from 14 pools assigned to two treatment categories: pools isolated by long-riffles (> 40m) and those by short riffles (< 10m). Repeatedly snorkeling each pool for three days in 1995 and 1997, we discovered significant effects of isolation. Generally, fish moved frequently among habitats (10-50%); however, combined movement from short-riffle into adjacent pools was six-times higher (24%) than movement from long-riffle pools (4%). Further, fish in short-riffle pools moved up and downstream with equal frequency, whereas those in long-riffle pools moved three-times more often downstream. Consistent with these results, we also found that assemblages in long-riffle pools were more stable than those in short-riffle pools (overall percent similarity, 87 vs 72%). 21917: Etheostoma rubrum is endemic to the Bayou Pierre system of west-central Mississippi and juveniles and adults are virtually restricted to riffles underlain with coarse substrata. 21918: The traditional approach in developing recovery plans for endangered species has been to directly sample the imperiled species. Utilizing surrogate species, however, provides a direct estimate of the imperiled species' biology while minimizing the impacts of direct sampling. For example, the Vermilion darter, Etheostoma chermocki, occurs in 11.5 kilometers of Turkey Creek, Jefferson County, Alabama. Although relatively common throughout its range, urban development continues to deteriorate conditions within the watershed. The surrogate method permits construction of a habitat suitability model using the sister species. This model incorporates multivariate statistical methods which identifies variables (e.g., discharge, habitat type, dominant substrate type, water pH, conductivity, temperature, relative abundance) that will be entered into a GIS spatial database. This model will then be tested on the surrogate prior to its application on the target species. 21919: The Peel-Harvey Estuary, located in south-western Australia has become very eutrophic since the early 1970s. 21920: Biology of the greater redhorse was studied in the middle reaches of the Grand River, Ontario from 1995 to 1997. 21921: Artificial reefs currently play only a minor role in fisheries or ecosystem management. The most notable example is their use in the spiny lobster fishery. Further examination of the role that artificial reefs can play in fisheries management needs to be explored. An example may be with regard to facilitating recruitment of juvenile and young adult serranid fishes (grouper and seabass) from inshore grassbeds to offshore, natural reefs. Further, artificial reefs can play a significant role in sanctuary and marine reserve programs. Moreover, purposeful and timed exploitation/rehabilitation of fish assemblages through artificial reefs may help sustain both fisheries and fish assemblages. Artificial reefs may not be effective in habitat mitigation where natural habitat has been destroyed. Information on the complete role that reefs play in trophic dynamics therefore needed. Additionally, an understanding of the time and spatial scales necessary to effect management objectives is essential. While, most artificial reef research, to date, has been directed toward fish and fish assemblages, additional insight into ecological processes and large scale ecosystem management may be gleaned through their study. In the future, artificial reefs construction and deployment design should be directed toward adding to our knowledge base to better manage nearshore and coastal ecosystems. Interagency, interstate, and international cooperation are the cornerstones for this endeavor. Both the positive and negative features of artificial reef deployment as a management tool need to be understood before they are generally accepted as a ecosystem management alternative.

21922: A website (http://www.ims.usm.edu/~musweb/endanger.html) has been created that provides information on vertebrate and invertebrate species potentially at risk in the Gulf of Mexico and adjoining coastal habitats. The website was developed as a means to disseminate the results of a workshop on the identification of potentially endangered species in the Gulf and to establish research needs for these species through a cooperative agreement between the US Gulf of Mexico Program and Gulf Coast Research Laboratory Museum. Detailed information is provided for 78 species, including 24 fish, 3 amphibians, and 8 reptiles. Data include synonyms, nomenclatural remarks, distinguishing features, similar species, species photographs, summaries of species biology, distribution, size, scientific basis for assessment of risk, status of gulf populations, and bibliographies. For fishes, online distributional maps and extensive archival records for each species were compiled through the assistance of many collections, most notably those of the five gulf states. These compilations were used to assess historical changes in species distributions. A bibliography of over 8,500 papers dealing with endangered species and related topics is also available, as well as links to other related websites. Extensions are directed toward more structured data collection, standardized online databasing, and inclusion of non-indigenous species so that information can readily accessed for management and educational purposes.
