21923: The notochord of the lamprey is a solid cylindrical organ consisting of a cellular medulla surrounded by an extracellular fibrous sheath and an elastic externa. The base of the medulla consists of a layer of columnar cells with an extensive network of rough endoplasmic reticulum and mitochondria. The cytoplasm of these cells also contains distinct lipid droplets and a peripheral network of intermediate filaments. The vacuoles in the cells located in the middle of the medulla are reinforced with a peripheral network of intermediate filaments. These cells are interconnected with numerous desmosomes. Lipid droplets and huge deposits of glycogen granules are also observed in the vacuolated cells. The fibrous sheath is made of several layers of collagen fibers. Interspersed between the collagen layers are deposits of extracellular matrix similar to that found in the elastic externa. The elastic externa is an amorphous layer of extracellular matrix that appears to be secreted by the fibroblasts and chondroblasts that surround the periphery of the notochord. There are several differences in the organization of the lamprey notochord when compared to the fine structure of the sturgeon and lungfish notochord (J. Morphol. 1998). These differences may have functional and phylogenetic implications that remain to be determined.

21924: Remoras (Echeneididae: Carangoidei) are medium sized, specialized pelagic fishes, inhabiting the warm water of the world. Remoras are found in close association with certain marine animals and inanimate objects. In all cases remoras use their sucking disc to attach to smooth surfaces. An osteological examination of cleared and stained remoras reveals that the disc is homologous with the dorsal fin of other percoids. The disc is composed of 4 structures: proximal, medial and distal pterygiophores, and the dorsal spines. These 4 structures are serially repeated to form the disc. The dorsal spine is reduced in size and enclosed in the fin membrane. The paired distal pterygiophore forms the denticulated laminae, and also supports the spine. The medial pterygiophore forms the perimeter of the disc, and supports the laminae forming a hinged joint which allows rotation. The proximal pterygiophore supports the entire unit, it connects to both the laminae and the medial pterygiophore. Each of these units is connected to the previous one by the proximal pterygiophore. The remora attaches itself by pressing the disc against a surface and rotating the distal pterygiophore around the hinged joint. This increases the volume of the sealed chamber creating a partial vacuum.

21925: The postembryonic development of the cartilaginous cephalic skeleton in Solea solea (Linne) was observed from hatching to the juvenile stage. Fry were trypsin-cleared and alcian-blue stained. At hatching, S. solea displays no cartilaginous structure. On day 3, the fry exhibit trabecular bars, Meckel's cartilages, palatoquadrates, hyosymplectics, hyoid bars, the first two ceratobranchials and basibranchials 1-3. On day 4, ceratobranchials 3 and 4 form. On day 12, short taeniae marginales are formed on the well-developed otic capsules and the branchial basket is nearly complete. On day 14, cartilage reduction begins as the posterior part of the trabecula communis separates from the otic capsules. On day 18, metamorphosis begins. The tectum posterius completes posteriorly the braincase dome. On day 20, the left eye moves to the median crest of the head and the right eye shifts a bit downwards. Consequently, displacement of the right eye induces a deformation extending to the right pterygoid process. On day 23, both eyes are located on the same side. On day 29, cartilage reduction affects the hyosymplectics; it continues with the first two ceratobranchials on day 32 and with the otic capsules on day 40.

21926: Xenopoecilius oophorus is a member of the basal clade of Adrianichthyidae. In order to determine the size and shape of brain regions in these fishes I used a 3-dimensional computer reconstruction system (TRI 3.10). To preserve the original size of structures specimens were immersion-fixed in 10% formalin and brains sectioned at 30 um on a cryostat. Outlines of 180 serial sections were traced to calculate the volume of one whole brain and six brain regions; olfactory bulbs (BO), telencephala (TE), optic tecta (TO), inferior lobes (IL), cerebellum (CE), and facial lobes (FL). Volumetric estimates from sampling every section were compared with estimates from sampling each 2nd, 4th and 8th section, as well as from ocular micrometry using linear measurements taken under a dissecting microscope. Estimates from section sampling and ocular micrometry did not differ significantly from the complete volumetric values. Estimates from ocular micrometry were derived from the ellipsoid model [V=1/6 pi*lwd] (l=length, w=width, and d=depth), except for the TO, which was estimated from [V=SA*T] (SA=surface area, T=thickness). Estimates of total brain size derived by measuring the linear distance between the anterior margin of the telencephalon and the obex did not differ significantly from estimates derived from weighing brains.

21927: According to Lindsey (1975), pleomerism is a correlation among related animal species between their numbers of meristic parts and their characteristic body sizes. Lindsey found a striking tendency for vertebral number to be positively correlated with maximum length in many families of fish; however, he did not find the same correlation among 36 species of the family Gobiidae in his analysis. Data on the maximum recorded size, numbers of vertebrae, fin-rays (in dorsal, anal, and pectoral fins), and scales in longitudinal row were taken from published reviews of the gobiid species occurring in the Indo-West-Pacific (120 species), South African (107), North East Atlantic (73), Black Sea (26) regions. Not only vertebral numbers, but all other counts appeared to be positively correlated with size of gobiid species in the four regions. Taxonomic applications of this phenomena and possible evolutionary explanations (e.g., life history correlates, structure of heritable morphological variation) are discussed.

21928: Fishes use their pectoral fins for a variety of locomotor functions including providing thrust for rectilinear movement. Most previous analyses of pectoral fin swimming in fishes have focused on the Perciformes, a relatively derived group. In this study we examine pectoral fin swimming in Polypterus palmas, Lepisosteus platostomus, and Amia calva, representing three basal clades of ray-finned fishes. Both forward and reverse swimming are analyzed to reflect the wide range of behaviors during which fishes use their pectoral fins. Anatomical changes which have occurred in the pectoral fin complex include duplication of musculature and the formation of a specialized fin ray to act as the leading edge of the fin. Kinematically, the frequencies of fin beats and three-dimensional excursions of the fin differ greatly between species. Electromyograms reveal differences in the duration, relative timing, and amplitude of activity in the pectoral muscles suggesting that motor patterns during swimming are not highly conserved in these taxa. These data are compared with information from more derived taxa to trace the evolution of pectoral fin swimming in actinopterygians.

21929: Comparative osteology of the nominal species Campostoma anomalum was investigated across most of its geographic range in North America. Considerable variation was found associated with the food cropping and food processing mechanisms (jaws, pharyngeals) and bones associated with the operation of these structures. Transformations in character states (using Campostoma ornatum and Dionda diaboli as outgroups) were found in the jaws, pharyngeals, suspensorium, opercular series, sphenotic, ethmoid, cranial roof and vertebral number. Results from the skeletal analysis were interpreted as follows. Two broadly defined groups were recognized. One, represented by Campostoma anomalum pullum, is widespread across the glaciated mid-section of North America and southward in the plains region. The second is a complex of forms (represented in the upper Ohio Valley by Campostoma a. anomalum) distributed in the Ohio River basin and peripheral areas to the east, south and west. The stonerollers found in the northern portions of the Ohio Valley can be pullum, anomalum or possible intermediates between the two depending on the drainage system. The largescale stoneroller, C. 'oligolepid', distributed in the Ozark uplands is a western component of the anomalum complex that is related to the similar but slightly more derived Tennessee-Cumberland stoneroller. The stoneroller that dominates the Tennessee-Cumberland is the most derived form of the anomalum complex. It has peripheral (extensions?) in the Green River, New River and on the gulf and east slopes. The name C. a. michauxi Fowler might apply to this form. Two of the most recognizable populations within the anomalum complex have smaller distributional ranges. One is found in the Roanoke-James and the other in the Ouachita drainage.

21930: Sperm competition is one vehicle by which males compete with each other for reproductive success. This paper examines sperm competition between the specialized cuckolder and parental male life histories of bluegill sunfish (Lepomis macrochirus). First, we find that the investment in total sperm production is higher in cuckolders than parentals and within cuckolders, males that have higher sperm production obtain higher fertilization success. Second, the longevity of sperm is lower in cuckolders than parentals. The alternative male reproductive life histories of bluegill therefore utilize sperm in different ways to compete for reproductive success. Cuckolders invest in quantity because they always face sperm competition, while parentals invest in quality because they only rarely face sperm competition. We compare these findings to those in other fishes by analyzing differences in sperm competition intensities and sperm quantity-quality tradeoffs.

21931: Sturgeons (Osteichthyes: Acipenseridae) are evolutionary relicts with a wide distribution in the northern hemisphere. The historical biogeography of their association with their diverse assemblage of host specific parasites is explored using phylogenetic systematics and information from geology, paleontology and paleogeography. The patterns indicate historical exchanges with a variety of host taxa and low levels of conspeciation, resulting in small clades of widely distributed parasite species. Sister taxa of parasites generally exhibit allopatric patterns associated with discrete landmasses and basins. A trans-Atlantic track involving Acipenser oxyrhynchus and A. sturio and a trans-Pacific track involving A. medirostris are evident. The parasite relationships also support a historical connection between North America and North Asian freshwater sturgeons (A. fulvescens and A. baeri or their ancestors) and the biogeographical and phylogenetic relationship of A. fulvescens and A. brevirostrum. Based on these parascript studies, it is hypothesized that a former contiguous distribution of Palaeartic and Neartic sturgeons was fragmented by climatic and tectonic events in the Tertiary causing displacement of the lake sturgeon lineage and its association with the Gulf of Mexico drainages.

21932: Surgeonfishes harbor a group of gut symbionts that include the largest known Eubacteria (cell lengths of 30 um to >500 um). Because the bacteria are acquired after larval surgeonfishes settle from the plankton, the fish/symbiont system in the Hawaiian Archipelago and other north Pacific locations provides an opportunity to address questions about evolution of host and symbionts within and among hosts, within and among islands, and among island systems. We have surveyed microbes in host surgeonfishes from Hawaii, Maui, Oahu, Kauai, French Frigate Shoals, Pearl & Hermes, and Midway Islands in the Hawaiian Archipelago, as well as from the Red Sea, Great Barrier Reef, Tuvalu, Moorea (French Polynesia), Ishigaki Island (Japan) and Gulf of California. A variety of structural morphs of the bacteria, differing in maximum size, cell shape, and the number and mode of formation of daughter cells, have been recorded from all sites except the Gulf. There appears to be considerable consistency in morphs occupying particular host species among the Hawaiian islands, but little consistency among island systems in terms of morphs occupying given host species. Preliminary molecular studies suggest local divergence of microbes within a single host, at least for widely separated localities.

21934: Parasites may play an important role in fish life history and mating system evolution. This paper examines parasite loads in a natural colony of bluegill sunfish (Lepomis macrochirus). All 8 parasite-types were quantified in selected tissues of over 200 females, cuckolders and parentals (n=16,438 parasites). Females and cuckolders have fewer parasites than do parental males. Parental males that obtain nest sites within the colony have fewer parasites than unsuccessful parental males. Thus, parasites apparently determine parental male opportunity to breed, and sexual selection for delayed maturation in parental males increases their average parasite loads. The evolution of the mating system and life histories in this fish is therefore subject to forces of selection from parasites.

21935: Lampetra aepyptera is a widespread species of non-parasitic lamprey found throughout the eastern United States. Previous studies have shown that certain populations of this lamprey exhibit heterochrony, by acheiving sexual maturity without completing metamorphosis. A preliminary survey of allozyme variation was performed to evaluate the extent of genetic differentiation among populations exhibiting either normal metamorphosis or truncated head development. The products of 22 loci were surveyed. Highly significant differentiation was observed among populations. A population from western Kentucky (Terrapin Creek) was highly differentiated from eastern Kentucky and Ohio populations, included several fixed allele differences. Because no metamorphosed adults have ever been collected from Terrapin Creek, it appears to be a new paedomorphic species. Furthermore, allele frequencies among the Terrapin Creek size classes were not different, suggesting variable time to reproduction in this population. The eastern Kentucky population (Big Sinking Creek) exhibits some evidence of incomplete metamorphosis. The presently recognized least brook lamprey appears to contain multiple species with a complex pattern of intra- and interspecific heterochrony. Additional allozyme and morphological studies are underway.

21936: Reef fish assemblages are strongly influenced by reef structure. In areas where visibility is poor, specific visual census methods are necessary to determine the fish community structure. This work, part of a broader study of Brazilian reef fishes community structure, aimed to establish specific visual census methods to determine the fish community structure in rocky reefs, areas characterized by high turbidity, strong currents and irregular substrate. Five strip-transect protocols (5m depth dives) were made; 5 x 2m/intensive search without defined time, 10 x 2m/5min, 20 x 4m/5min, 40 x 4m/10min and 50 x 4m/10min. An inventory of the fishes and a comparative study of the community structure was made at Marine State Parks Laje de Santos (24° 19' S and 46° 11' W) and at Alcatrazes Archipelago (24° 06' S and 45° 42' W), off Sao Paulo State. Diversity index indicated that the transect 50 x 4m/10min is the most adequate for the studied areas, and that species number nearly stabilized at 40 x 4m/10min. 28 species were censused and protocols were produced for each one. Laje de Santos showed 19 species and Alcatrazes 21 species. Twelve censused species occurred in both areas.

21937: Two key resources are generally thought to limit salmonid populations in streams: the supply of food and the amount of suitable space within the channel. However, the relative influence of these limiting factors can change seasonally. Both food and habitat availability can affect individual fitness, but to what extent does each factor influence salmonid growth and survival on a seasonal basis? I performed a summer field experiment to directly test the effect of food and cover on growth and survival of stream-dwelling coastal cutthroat trout (Oncorhynchus clarki clarki). Using a 2x2 factorial design, I manipulated food and cover in stream enclosures containing individually marked trout. Fish receiving food addition experienced growth rates more than 25 times higher than those of unfed fish. There was no effect of cover on either growth or survival. These results indicate that trout were severely food-limited during summer. During winter, I combined a mark-recapture study of fish with stream habitat surveys to determine the extent to which habitat complexity limits growth and survival. Finally, to address how summer growth affects over-winter survival, I monitored fish released back into the stream from the summer experiment throughout winter.

21940: Spatial and temporal patterns in trophic structure of fishes from Agua Nanci creek, upper Parana river basin (Brazil) were assessed. Three monthly samples were taken from May 1996 to January 1997 using electrofishing, in three segments of the creek (near the spring, middle of its extension, and near the mouth). Food spectrum was obtained by analyzing gastric contents, with occurrence and volumetric methods, using the alimentary index. Trophic categories were established based on: the main food item, the interpretation of the Detrended Correspondence Analysis - DCA, and Average-linkage clustering (Euclidean Distance-UPGMA). The relative abundance of the food resources was estimated based on stomach content analysis. Diversity and food resources increased towards the mouth and were related to the conservation of riparian vegetation and to longitudinal hydro-morphological gradients of the creek. Temporal variations in food resources were associated with seasonal prey and hydrological cycles, thereby influencing the proportions of dominant trophic categories. Omnivores predominated in the upper part and benthivores near the mouth. Piscivores and detritivores presented low biomass. Longitudinal distribution of the trophic categories did not follow the river continuum concept, but was more related to food resources, habitat heterogeneity and the conservation conditions in each segment of the creek.

21941: Radiated tortoises are found within a limited range of spiny forest habitat in South Western Madagascar. Specific observations on the tortoises were made from November 23, 1997 to December 4, 1997. The majority of observed tortoises were found along a 75-km stretch of road between Route 10 near Betioky, and the fishing village of Beheloka. A total of 32 live tortoises, ranging in age from a juvenile that was a few years old (CL=12 cm) to a large adult male (CL=37.5 cm), were recorded. The mean carapace length was 25.5 cm. Tortoise weights ranged from 0.59 to 10 kg (mean=4.5 kg). The tortoises appeared healthy with no visible deformities or ecto-parasites. Some of the data collected include temperature, size, gular scute length, and anal scute length. The latter two were collected in order to examine sexual dimorphism. The author spent most of November 1997 in Madagascar as part of a preliminary fact-finding trip sponsored by Conservation International (Washington, D.C.).

21942: Decline in frog and tadpole populations may alter trophic structures and ecosystems. During summer 1997 I investigated impacts of tadpole populations on food webs in ponds of Yellowstone National Park. The field component of this project involved two phases - experimental manipulations in enclosures and landscape-level comparison of unmanipulated ponds with and without tadpoles. In separate experiments, I stocked three blocks of enclosures with or without tadpoles of Rana luteiventris and Bufo boreas. In the experiment with Bufo boreas tadpoles, I compared their impacts with those of freshwater snails. Every two weeks until tadpole metamorphosis I measured tadpole and snail length, and collected samples of algal biomass. Results showed the Rana luteiventris tadpoles depressed algal biomass after two weeks of growth, but not after four weeks. Bufo boreas tadpoles did not depress algal biomass, but snails did. In the landscape-level project I compared eleven unmanipulated ponds, five with tadpoles and six without. This comparison did not show a statistically significant impact of tadpoles on algal biomass. Results of the two phases of this project suggest that enclosures accurately mimicked conditions in whole ponds, and that tadpole grazing had a complex influence on algal biomass, rather than a direct negative impact.

21943: Low-head dams are a possible means to control spawning migration of parasitic sea lamprey, Petromyzon marinus, in tributary streams of the Laurentian Great lakes. This would reduce the need for chemical control. We studied the effects of low-head dams on stream fish communities by comparing streams with dams to paired reference streams without dams. We used electrofishing to sample streams above and below dams, and corresponding sections of barrier streams at three different seasons during the year. Fish were marked according to the location of first capture. The dams appear to block upstream movements of sea lamprey. Movements of fish above and below the locations of dams, or corresponding sites on reference streams, did not differ among streams. Upstream movements of fish over dams was reduced, compared to reference streams. The longitudinal decrease in fish species diversity from downstream to upstream sections is greater for streams with dams than for matched reference streams. Our study identified fish species most vulnerable to the effects of low-head dams and suggested likely mechanisms for this impact.

21944: Little is known about the ecology of stream-dwelling coho salmon (Oncorhynchus kisutch) in the Lake Superior drainage. Unlike in their native range of the Pacific Northwest, Lake Superior coho salmon inhabit streams characterized by low winter flows and highly variable summer flows. Because high stream flows can profoundly influence fish behavior and distribution, we hypothesized in this study that the winter ecology of coho in Lake Superior streams would differ from patterns described for pacific populations. In snorkeling surveys completed in winter 1998, we examined the distribution and social organization of over-wintering coho in simple (no cover) and complex pools of a Lake Superior tributary in Wisconsin. In all habitats, coho occupied focal positions in the main channel; however, fish were more tightly distributed and closer to the streambanks in simple pools. Aggressive interactions also were more common in simple pools although dominance hierarchies were observed in the majority of all pools. These results are in sharp contrast with research findings from pacific streams, which generally show coho moving to protected habitats and becoming less aggressive with the onset of high flows in winter. This study provides new insights into the behavioral plasticity of coho salmon and should aid in efforts to manage Great Lake populations.

21945: We assessed how biotic and abiotic factors influence the local diversity (alpha diversity) of fish communities in two rainforest streams (Itingucu e Tetequera) in the southeastern Brazil. These two streams rise in Itatins mountain, approximately at the altitude of 800 m and run into other plain rivers near the ocean. Tide influences is noticed at the lower stretches in both streams. Four sampling sites were chosen in each stream based on local physiographic features along the overall length. Fishes were collected by fykenets, dipnets, sieves and gillnets. Physico-chemical parameters (pH, temperature, conductivity, water current velocity, dissolved oxygen) and altitude were measured using portable equipment. The total of 40 species were obtained. Twenty-nine are typical of freshwater whereas 11 are considered marine species. We collected 33 species in Itingucu stream, being 22 restrict to that area. In Tetequera 18 species were captured but only 7 were of local occurrence. The ichthyofauna of both communities showed altitudinal gradient and were formed through the processes of species addition and substitution. Species addition is more evident in the upper and medium stretches of the streams and is influence by biotic factors (vacant niche occupation and resources partitioning) and abiotic factors (physico-chemical parameters variations). On the other hand, the substitution process was more evident in the streams lower stretches as a consequence of ecological equivalence. Therefore, in these patches, abiotic factors are the main agent influencing the structure of these communities. The species diversity of each community was analyzed based on the relation between species abundance and number. The Whittaker Plot analysis of both communities suggest that they follow log series and log normal distribution.
21946: The assemblage of rainforest snakes of the Manaus region, Central Amazon, was studied from 1991 to 1995. Fieldwork resulted in nearly 800 snakes of 66 forest species. Snake activity was markedly lower during the dry season. Of the 61 species for which information is available, 43% were primarily terrestrial, 31% fossorial and/or cryptozoic, 20% arboreal, and 6% aquatic. Nearly all inactive snakes were found on the vegetation. In relation to time of activity, 41% of 62 species seem to be strictly diurnal, 21% strictly nocturnal, and 38% both diurnal and nocturnal. The commonest prey were lizards (consumed by 58% of the species), frogs (39%), mammals (23%), birds (18%), and snakes (16%). A cluster analysis combining data on microhabitat use, diel activity and diet resulted in 'guilds' encompassing mostly closely related species, but also distantly related ones that converge in habits. These patterns clearly reflect the relative contribution of colubrid lineages in the assemblage, indicating that historical factors (phylogeny and biogeography) may have played and important role in determining the current organisation of this forest snake assemblage. However, current predation pressure and differential prey availability in the forest tridimensional space seem to be important in determining current patterns of microhabitat use.

21947: The genus Bothrops is composed by at least five monophyletic clades. We present original data on the feeding habits of 12 species, encompassing all five clades. All species in the alternatus group seem to be mammal specialists, whose juveniles are relatively large and stout and lack pale tail tips (used to lure ectothermic prey in other species). All species of the four remaining groups are euryphagic and ontogenetic shift in prey types seems to occur in all: juveniles feed mostly on frogs and lizards, adults mainly on mammals (except for the isolated B. insularis, whose adults feed mostly on birds). Juveniles of these euryphagic species are relatively small and thin, and their tail tips are distinctly coloured (retained in adults of B. bilineatus and B. insularis). The sit-and-wait foraging tactic is the most commonly used by Bothrops, although all species may occasionally forage actively. Our results indicate that euryphagy, sit-and-wait foraging, ontogenetic shift in prey type and distinctly coloured tail tips associated with caudal luring are all plesiomorphic characters in the genus Bothrops. 21948: The Nerodia clarkii complex is one that ranges from Eastern Texas, along the Gulf Coast to Volusia County, Florida. 21949: Seasonal variation in sex ratio is well documented for many species of turtles, and is largely attributable to a seasonal increase in temperature. 21950: Length and age of 53 wood frogs, Rana sylvatica, from Kuujjuarapik in northern Quebec (55-17' N) was compared with similar data from populations of other southern latitudes. 21951: Dorsal color pattern in snakes is remarkably variable within and between species, providing a good opportunity to study the adaptive significance of coloration. 21952: Herbivory is a derived feeding characteristic that has evolved independently several times in all the major phyla and classes of metazoans. Bony fishes are no exceptions to this. 21953: Spatial and temporal patterns in the distribution, composition and fish assemblage structure and their relation to physical gradients were assessed. 21954: Both biomass and abundance data are commonly utilized in characterization of ecological system dynamics; however, questions exist as to which approach is best-suited for long-term studies. 21955: Central to the hierarchical theory is the concept that organisation results from differences in process rates. 21956: The evolution of viviparity in the genus Sceloporus is associated with a shift from the spring mating and late summer hatching observed for oviparous species to fall mating and spring birth observed for viviparous species. We studied the reproductive cycles of two populations of S. aeneus and three of S. bicanthalis. The timing of the reproductive cycle of S. aeneus was as expected for an oviparous species. The timing of the reproductive cycle of S. bicanthalis, was, however, intermediate between oviparous and typical viviparous species. Like S. aeneus, hatchlings of S. bicanthalis are produced in late summer. More like typical viviparous species, however, mating by S. bicanthalis occurs in the winter. In the scalaris group, thus, the evolution of viviparity is associated with an earlier initiation of the breeding season (spring to previous winter), but the shift from fall to spring parition occurs after viviparity becomes stablished. 21957: A marked sexual dimorphism was observed in the height of the second dorsal fin in the Patagonian shore fish Patagonotothen sima. 21958: The hatching success of bog turtle (Clemmys muhlenbergii) eggs from a single population was examined at a site in eastern Pennsylvania. 21959: The evolution of viviparity in reptiles is presumably associated with a reduced clutch size and increased relative clutch mass. 21960: The Indo-Pacific scorpaeniform family, Caracanthidae, contains a single genus of four or five known species. These fish are small-sized and live cryptically within highly branching corals. 21961: We will briefly review the development of the radio-acoustic positioning system (RAP) and describe the simultaneously tracking of five white sharks by the RAP over a three-week period during Oct.-Nov. 1988. 21964: The investigation of calling energetics in frogs provides an opportunity to integrate studies of behavioral performance with whole animal physiology, muscle structure, and muscle biochemistry. 21965: Advertisement calls of anurans usually have one or two emphasized frequency bands, which match fairly well with the maximum frequency sensitivity of one or the other, or both, of the two auditory organs, the basilar and amphibian papillae. 21966: Male Pacific treefrogs, Hyla regilla, use advertisement and encounter calls to regulate inter-male spacing within breeding choruses. These aggressive thresholds are plastic; i.e. males resume advertisement calling (accommodate) to repeated presentation of advertisement calls at amplitudes 4 dB above their aggressive threshold. Correspondingly, a male's aggressive threshold for the advertisement call is positively correlated with the maximum amplitude of advertisement calls of neighbors, measured at the focal male's position. The aggressive thresholds of males for the encounter call also are plastic but are not significantly correlated with the maximum call amplitude of their neighbors. This disjunction stems from the fact that males in stable choruses are not exposed to supra-threshold encounter calls. Accommodation to one call type fails to significantly alter a male's aggressive threshold to the other call type. Plasticity of aggressive thresholds, like plasticity of aggressive signalling, appears to be important in balancing the costs and benefits of aggressive behavior. The capacity of males to selectively accommodate to the advertisement or encounter call supports the hypothesis that these two call types are processed, in part, by discrete neural 'channels'. Because these two call types are highly similar spectrally, selective accommodation cannot result from sensory adaptation in the periphery. The two call types however, differ markedly in their temporal structure, particularly their pulse repetition rate. These observations support the notion that separate temporal filters exist in the central nervous system for processing these two call types. Recent neurophysiological studies have provided insight into the mechanisms that underlie this temporal pattern recognition and discrimination.

21967: Ectothermy is the norm among animals. It is known that aspects of both acoustic signal production and reception in ectotherms are temperature-dependent. 21968: In this paper I present an integrative model that accounts for the relationship between intra- and interspecific variation in male advertisement call characteristics in frogs and intra- and interspecific differences in androgen and corticosteroid levels. 21970: The phylogeny, biogeography, and evolution of troglobitic characters were investigated in the Amblyopsidae using DNA sequence data from the mitochondrial gene ND2. 21971: Explorations last year revealed a second locality for Prietella lundbergi, or a closely related form, in an isolated, 50 m deep sump about 50 km north of the type locality in southernmost Tamaulipas. Results of the analysis indicate a minimum can occur, and is most evident in systems with a physically long salinity gradient. Beta diversity calculations confirmed the region of highest species turnover was displaced upstream from the minimum (near 0-2 ppt), and coincides with the most severe changes in ionic ratios. Hence, distance to source pools of marine and freshwater taxa appears to interact with salinity preferences to establish the minimum. Excursions from most favorable habitats by a highly mobile species appears spatially similar to recruitment survival in sessile invertebrates, and may explain the similarity in pattern between the two groups.
